tagline.text: A steel arch across the strait, joining the promise of Leyte and Samar

location.label: Location
location.text: Tacloban City, Leyte – Santa Rita, Samar

items.credit: Oscar Rasson / Public domain / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A bridge about
long linking Tacloban on Leyte Island with Santa Rita on Samar Island, it was the longest bridge over the sea in the Philippines for nearly half a century. Since opening in
it has become a symbol of Eastern Visayas, with beautiful views over the island-dotted San Juanico Strait and lovely night lighting.

San Juanico Bridge crosses the narrow sea passage known as the San Juanico Strait between Leyte and Samar islands. Linking Tacloban City on the Leyte side with Santa Rita on the Samar side, its total length of about

made it, for many years, the longest bridge over a sea strait in the Philippines. The main center span is a red-painted steel truss arch, instantly recognizable from a distance, with piers curving in an S-shape on either side as they carry the bridge across the strait.
Construction began in
and the bridge opened in

. It was built with Japanese loans and technical assistance, and the Marcos administration at the time promoted it as the "Bridge of Love," framed as a gift for First Lady Imelda, who hailed from Leyte. Opinions on its political symbolism are mixed, but there is no doubt about its historical significance: the bridge completed the Pan-Philippine Highway (Maharlika Highway) connecting Luzon through Samar to Leyte and on to Mindanao.
When super typhoon Haiyan (locally known as Yolanda) devastated Tacloban in

, the bridge did not collapse and served as a lifeline for relief supplies moving in and out. However, more than 50 years after opening, structural aging showed up, leading to an emergency load restriction in
May 2025
. After major reinforcement work, two-way traffic under a 15-ton limit resumed in
December 2025
. The government is now working to restore the original 33-ton load capacity within

From the bridge itself and the viewpoints on either side, you can take in scenery of islands large and small scattered across the strait, bangkas cutting through the current, and the mountains of Samar in the distance. It's an easy half-day addition to sightseeing in Tacloban, and a symbolic landmark that travelers crossing Eastern Visayas by road naturally pass through.

blocks.title: Viewing the full span from the Leyte-side park

children.text: From the viewpoint near the bridge's entrance on the Leyte side, you can see the bridge crossing the strait head-on. It's a great spot for photos that capture both the arch section and the curving piers together.

Many travelers walk along the narrow footpaths on either side of the bridge as far as the arch section. You can look down at the swirling strait and small islands below, but stay alert since it runs close to traffic, and it may be closed off during construction.

blocks.title: Sunset viewed from the Samar side

children.text: From the viewpoint on the Santa Rita side, you can look at the bridge facing the direction the sun sets behind the mountains of Leyte. The red sky at dusk paired with the steel arch's silhouette is striking.
Once the sun sets, the bridge's scenic lights switch on and change color. Viewed from the Tacloban-side coast or a viewpoint park, it looks as if a ribbon of light is floating over the strait.
Asking a local boatman lets you ride a bangka under the bridge to explore the strait's small islands and mangroves. Since currents in the strait are fast, do this on a calm-weather morning.

blocks.title: Tacloban's Santo Niño Shrine and museum

children.text: The Santo Niño Shrine and Heritage Museum, built by Imelda Marcos, offers a glimpse into the opulence of power in the 1970s–80s. Visiting alongside the bridge helps put its history in context.
On Palo beach south of Tacloban stands a bronze statue reenacting General MacArthur's landing on Leyte in
October 1944
. It's the site of the Battle of Leyte, a turning point in the Pacific War.

blocks.title: Visiting a memorial site of Typhoon Haiyan

children.text: In the Anibong area, a cargo ship swept ashore by the storm surge has been left as a memorial. It's a reminder of the tragedy of
and the city's resilience.

An efficient itinerary is to tour the Palo MacArthur Landing Memorial Park and the Anibong Haiyan memorial in the morning, visit the Santo Niño Shrine after lunch, and see the San Juanico Bridge at sunset and night in the late afternoon.
Philippine Airlines and Cebu Pacific fly several times daily from Manila to Tacloban Airport (TAC), taking about
1 hour 15 minutes
. There's also a direct flight from Cebu taking only about
50 minutes
. The airport is in the San Jose area southeast of downtown, about
15–20 minutes
from the city and about
30–40 minutes
from the bridge. Airport taxis and vans to downtown cost about

Long-distance buses to Tacloban from Manila's Cubao and Pasay terminals pass through the Bicol region, cross by ferry from Matnog port in Sorsogon to Allen port in Samar, then traverse Samar and cross the San Juanico Bridge to reach Tacloban. The whole trip takes about
22–26 hours
, costing about

. During periods of the bridge's load restrictions, large bus passengers have sometimes had to disembark in front of the bridge and transfer to smaller vehicles, so check the current operating arrangement before departing.
A common route is taking a fast ferry from Cebu to Ormoc (about
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours
), then a van to Tacloban (about
2–2 hours 30 minutes
). An overnight Cebu–Tacloban passenger ferry also operates but takes much longer.
From downtown Tacloban, jeepneys or multicabs bound for the bridge area (Santa Rita, Basey) let you off near the Leyte-side bridge entrance (about
20–30 minutes
, about
). To reach the Samar-side viewpoint, it's more convenient to take a Santa Rita/Basey-bound van or charter a tricycle or taxi. A half-day chartered vehicle costs about
Eastern Visayas faces the Pacific directly, making it one of the rainiest regions in the Philippines. There's no long, clear dry season, but
March
through
June
tends to be relatively clear with calm seas. From
November
to
January
, the northeast monsoon brings rain and cloudy days, and from
July
to
December
, the region is frequently in the path of typhoons.
Around
June
29–30, the Pintados-Kasadyaan Festival is held to mark Tacloban's Santo Niño feast day, filling the streets with dancers in traditional tattoo body paint. Around
October 20
, the Leyte Landing commemoration is held in Palo. The bridge is at its most beautiful from dusk through when the night lighting comes on, so a late-afternoon visit is recommended.

Downtown Tacloban is the most convenient place to stay. The old town around city hall and the Santo Niño church has small hotels at about
per night, while the coastal road toward the airport has mid-range hotels around
per night alongside shopping malls. Many hotels were rebuilt after Haiyan, so facilities are generally clean and modern.

Leyte's signature snacks are binagol, a taro-coconut-sugar mix steamed in a coconut shell, and moron, glutinous rice twisted with chocolate and wrapped in banana leaf. Both are sold everywhere from markets and terminals to souvenir shops, making popular gifts. As a coastal city, Tacloban has many seafood restaurants serving grilled fish and squid, crab dishes, and kinilaw (raw fish ceviche), and in the evening, barbecue skewer stalls line the seaside promenade area.
The bridge is best for photos from about
1 hour
before sunset through
30 minutes
after the lights come on.
A telephoto lens lets you frame the arch section tightly from the Leyte-side viewpoint park, while a wide-angle lens captures the bridge's full curve.
The footpath on the bridge is narrow with no shade at all at midday, so bring a hat and water and walk in the morning or late afternoon.
Downtown Tacloban has plenty of ATMs and malls, but small towns on the Samar side are mostly cash-only.
To continue on to the eastern Samar coast or the Marabut rock islands, take an early-morning van from Tacloban.
During bridge construction, lane closures and congestion can occur, so add at least
30 minutes
of buffer time when heading to the airport.
Drone footage can run into restrictions in the airport approach area and bridge security zones, so it's best not to fly without permission from the relevant authorities.
San Juanico Bridge has had ongoing reinforcement work and load restrictions since

. Pedestrian access, vehicle control, and large-vehicle procedures can change frequently, so check the latest notices from the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) and the local government before visiting.
On the bridge, vehicles pass quickly and winds are strong, so don't lean on the railing or step onto the roadway.
During typhoon season, strong winds can temporarily restrict bridge crossing, and flight cancellations are also common, so leave buffer time in your schedule.
The strait has very fast currents, making swimming or personal kayaking dangerous. Always wear a life vest when riding a bangka.
Construction zones, pier bases, and guard posts may restrict photography or access, so follow posted instructions.
Tacloban sees rising dengue cases during the rainy season, so use mosquito repellent.
